title: Influence of surface topology on fatigue of DED-Arc specimens: a NURBS-based 3D-FEA approach
abstract: Abstract Directed energy deposition with electric arc sources (DED-Arc) is an additive manufacturing (AM) technology for the production of metal components, particularly in the field of structural steel applications. Its ability to process high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steels using cost-effective wire feedstock is notable. However, the as-built surface of DED-Arc components is characterised by significant waviness and irregularities due to the nature of the layerwise deposition process. These surface features act as potential stress concentrators and can have a significant effect on fatigue performance. In this study, the influence of surface topology on the fatigue behaviour of DED-Arc-manufactured components of HSLA steels is investigated. Fatigue tests were conducted on specimens in both as-built and machined surface conditions to experimentally quantify the impact of surface waviness. High-resolution 3D scanning and reverse engineering using NURBS-based surface reconstruction were employed to accurately represent real geometries in finite element simulations. Local stress distributions were evaluated to determine fatigue notch factors related to surface waviness. Furthermore, the base material was characterised experimentally by fatigue tests and the results were used in a numerical framework to estimate the fatigue life. Combining the experimental fatigue data with simulation-based notch factor evaluation enabled the development of fatigue life estimation that accounts for manufacturing-induced surface effects. The findings demonstrate the necessity of considering real surface topologies in fatigue assessments and offer a basis for improved design and qualification of AM components.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Directed energy deposition using electric arc processes (DED-Arc), also known as wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM), has increasing relevance in the field of additive manufacturing (AM) for manufacturing steel components with high deposition rates and design flexibility [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ]. In structural and offshore applications, DED-Arc offers significant advantages in terms of material efficiency and geometrical freedom [ 6 ]. However, the as-built surface condition resulting from the layerwise deposition process often exhibits waviness, irregularities, and local notches, which can impair the performance of as-built components [ 7 ]. These surface features significantly influence crack initiation under cyclic loading. As a result, the fatigue strength of as-built specimens is typically reduced compared to conventionally manufactured or machined counterparts. Previous studies have shown that machined specimens manufactured by DED-Arc exhibit improved fatigue performance due to the elimination of geometrically induced stress concentrations [ 8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11 – 12 ]. While surface finishing methods such as milling or polishing can reduce this effect by removing critical surface features, the additional manufacturing step leads to an increase in production costs and may not be applicable to complex or internal geometries.

Shojai et al. [ 17 ,  18 – 19 ] applied reverse engineering techniques to assess the fatigue strength of corroded steel specimens by reconstructing the surface geometry using Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS)–based modelling. Their work demonstrates the applicability of reverse-engineered geometries for evaluating local stress distributions in components with irregular surface conditions, highlighting the relevance of NURBS for capturing geometrically complex features in fatigue analysis. There remains a need for research into the influence of as-built surface topology on fatigue strength, because the surface waviness can significantly depend on process parameters. Understanding these effects is essential for reliably assessing the fatigue performance of DED-Arc components.

This study combines high-resolution surface scanning, reverse engineering based on NURBS, and three-dimensional finite element simulations to quantify local stress concentrations in as-built DED-Arc specimens. Fatigue tests were performed on both machined and as-built specimens under identical loading conditions to evaluate the effect of surface topology on fatigue life. The experimentally determined material parameters and numerically derived fatigue stress concentration factors were used to develop a local fatigue estimation based on the actual surface geometry.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: Fatigue tests on machined and as-built specimens were carried out to assess the fatigue strength and to support the numerical analysis of surface-induced fatigue strength reduction. Machined specimens served to establish baseline fatigue properties and formed the basis for the fatigue life estimation in connection with the numerical investigations. As-built specimens were 3D-scanned, and the measured geometries were reconstructed using Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS) to create accurate finite element models. Fatigue stress concentration factors were derived from these simulations. Experimental tests on as-built specimens validated the numerical estimations by the magnitude of the fatigue stress concentration factors and the correspondence between predicted stress peaks and actual failure locations.

sections.heading: Specimen properties
paragraphs:
The fatigue specimens were extracted from thin walls produced via the DED-Arc process. This specimen orientation represents the lowest strength and was therefore selected as the critical condition [ 20 ]. All specimens were manufactured from feedstock material voestalpine Böhler AM80 HD (10NiMnMoCr8-7-6), a high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steel developed specifically for additive manufacturing applications. The DED-Arc deposition was carried out with a cold metal transfer (CMT) process, an interpass temperature below 200 °C and a specific energy input of 2.7 kJ/cm. In Table  1 , the process parameters used for manufacturing the walls from which the fatigue specimens were extracted are summarised.

Four thin walls were manufactured, from each of which six specimens were extracted, resulting in a total of 12 as-built and 12 machined specimens available for testing. A structured naming convention encoding the main experimental parameters was used to uniquely label each fatigue specimen (see Table  2 ).
 Table 2 Naming convention of fatigue specimens Surface condition Identifier of thin-walled component Orientation Number of specimens As-built 1 to 2 V = vertical 1 to 6 Machined 3 to 4 V = vertical 1 to 6

To investigate the influence of surface condition, two specimen surface conditions were considered, as-built and machined. The machined specimens were milled to a thickness of 3.5 mm to remove the surface waviness of all specimens and polished to achieve a defined surface finish. The thicknesses of the as-built specimens are provided in Table  5  in the Appendix. To prevent crack initiation at the specimen edges, the machined specimens were additionally chamfered by a milling machine with a radius of 0.5 mm to create a controlled edge radius. This radius was applied only to the machined specimens, as the as-built specimens exhibited an irregular wavy surface where a defined machining of the edge was not feasible. Furthermore, if cracks initiate at the edge, the results are only comparable to machined specimens to a limited extent. The geometry of the fatigue specimens is shown in Fig.  1 . Fig. 1 a  Fatigue specimens alignment from DED-Arc printed wall.  b  Cut-out geometry of fatigue specimen in mm

sections.heading: Test setup
paragraphs: The fatigue tests were performed in accordance with the specifications of DIN 50100 [ 21 ] under constant load amplitude and within the high cycle fatigue (HCF). Two different testing setups were used in order to account for the different surface conditions of the machined and as-built specimens. The tests were carried out under force control. All fatigue tests (machined and as-built specimens) were conducted under load control at a stress ratio of  R  = 0.1. Fatigue tests on the machined specimens were carried out using a Schenk 160 servo-hydraulic testing machine, where the load was introduced through hydraulic wedge grips clamping the specimen ends. The test setup for the machined specimens is shown in Fig.  2 . The testing machine has a maximum applied load capacity of 160 kN and a test frequency of 50 Hz. Fig. 2 Fatigue test setup (Schenk 160 kN) for machined specimens

Fatigue tests on the as-built specimens were performed using a servo-hydraulic actuator (MTS 204.63) with a maximum load capacity of 100 kN (see Fig.  3 ). The lower adapter was mounted with a rotational joint to permit free rotation about all axes to minimise unintended bending moments during testing. The contact-based load introduction via custom adapter elements was specifically designed to avoid damage to the rough as-built surfaces. The adapter is rigidly connected to the hydraulic cylinder and transfers the load to the specimen shoulders through contact pressure (see Fig.  3  (right)). The setup was validated in preliminary tests to ensure stable and repeatable loading conditions under cyclic fatigue. Fig. 3 Fatigue test setup (MTS 204.63) for as-built specimens

Additionally, a Digital Image Correlation (DIC) system was applied to monitor the deformation behaviour of the as-built surface during testing. However, the DIC data are not part of the evaluation presented in this work. For the as-built specimens tested on the servo-hydraulic machine, test frequencies between 30 and 50 Hz were applied.

Both test setups were chosen to ensure that the load introduction reflected uniaxial boundary conditions without introducing artificial stress concentrations and bending effects. While the machined specimens benefited from conventional clamping and well-defined contact surfaces, the as-built specimens required a tailored load transfer concept to accommodate surface irregularities and avoid damage during testing. This dual setup allowed for a reliable comparison of fatigue behaviour under consistent loading conditions despite differing surface states.

sections.heading: Numerical flowchart
paragraphs: The numerical investigation of surface-induced fatigue effects was based on a detailed workflow consisting of surface digitisation, geometry reconstruction, and finite element analysis, as illustrated in Fig.  4 . Fig. 4 Numerical flowchart of NURBS-based 3D-FEA

The process began with the capture of the three-dimensional geometry of the as-built specimen surface. The mesh alignment was carried out using CloudCompare v2.14.alpha. The resulting polygon mesh was subsequently processed using MeshLab 2023.12 and Fusion360 2024. In the next stage, the cleaned mesh was converted into a continuous surface using Rhino 8. This reverse engineering step was essential to avoid artificial sharp edges and mesh discontinuities that could lead to numerical singularities during stress analysis. The NURBS-based model was then used as input for the finite element simulations using Abaqus/Standard 2024. The final step involved the numerical evaluation of local stress concentration factors related to the surface topology.

sections.heading: 3D scanning as-built surface
paragraphs: The geometry of the as-built specimen surface was captured using a high-resolution structured-light scanner (Hexagon StereoScan neo R16.2), as shown in Fig.  5 . The specimen was mounted on a turntable using a clamping fixture to ensure stable positioning during scanning. A full 360° surface acquisition was achieved through 16 rotational increments, enabling the scanner to capture the specimen from 16 discrete perspectives without requiring manual alignment of individual scans. Before the scanning, the specimen surface was cleaned and coated with a matting spray (thickness of 10 µm) to reduce surface reflectivity and improve scan quality. Reference points were placed around the specimen to support the alignment of the multiple scans. The scanner was calibrated before the measurements, yielding a calibration accuracy of 4 µm. Fig. 5 3D scanning of fatigue specimen with high-resolution structured-light scanner (Hexagon StereoScan neo R16.2)

The resulting scan data serve as the geometric basis for the following numerical analysis. Initially, the scanner generates a point cloud of the specimen surface, capturing the geometry with high resolution. Based on this point cloud, a polygon mesh is automatically created and exported as an STL file. This file format provides a suitable input for reverse engineering and further surface processing required for finite element modelling. The maximum resolution of the polygon mesh is 12 µm based on the used working distance.

sections.heading: Reverse engineering
paragraphs: The initial surface representation obtained from the 3D scan is a polygon mesh, which approximates the measured point cloud through a linear interpolation of adjacent vertices (see Fig.  6 ). The mesh consists of numerous flat triangular elements, resulting in a piecewise linear and geometrically discontinuous surface. When the polygon mesh was directly used in the finite element simulations, these artificial edges and corners introduce non-physical stress concentrations that may dominate the local stress field. Fig. 6 Polygon mesh based on the point cloud and NURBS surface reconstruction

As a consequence, it becomes difficult to isolate the actual influence of the measured surface topology, since any local variation in stress may be driven more by meshing artefacts than by the underlying geometry. To address this issue, the polygon mesh is converted into a smooth and continuous geometry using NURBS to eliminate the discontinuous surface. They are mathematical representations used to model smooth and complex geometries in computer-aided design. They define curves and surfaces using control points, basis functions, and optional weighting factors, allowing precise control over shape and continuity.

sections.heading: Numerical analysis
paragraphs: To evaluate the influence of the as-built surface profile on the local stress distribution, numerical simulations were carried out using three-dimensional finite element analysis (3D-FEA). Due to the surface waviness, local bending effects and stress concentrations occur, resulting in a multiaxial stress state within the parallel section, which is the highly stressed central region of the specimen with a constant width of 13 mm (see Fig.  1 b). A 2D simulation is therefore not sufficient to map the multiaxial stress state. The applied modelling approach allows for the assessment of stress concentration factors relevant to fatigue initiation under realistic surface conditions. The input geometry for the simulations was derived from the reverse-engineered NURBS surface model, which accurately represents the scanned as-built specimen geometry.

sections.heading: Boundary conditions
paragraphs: The radial constraint reflects the boundary conditions of the experimental adapter (see Fig.  3 ), as the contact-based load introduction in the test setup allows vertical deformation of the specimen. Furthermore, lateral displacement was restricted in the simulation to reflect the experimental setup, where the specimen is laterally supported by clamped plates. The applied load corresponds to the average cross-sectional area in the parallel section, computed as the specimen’s average thickness multiplied by the constant width of 13 mm. As a result, the computed stress field directly represents the elastic static stress concentration factor. The geometry was partitioned into multiple sections to enable local control of the mesh density via seed definitions. Smaller elements were applied along the as-built surface in the parallel section. In contrast, coarser elements were used in the non-critical regions outside the area of interest to reduce computational effort while maintaining overall model stability.

sections.heading: Mesh sensitivity study
paragraphs: To assess the influence of element size and surface representation on the calculated stress concentration, a mesh sensitivity study was carried out using a simplified numerical model containing only the parallel section of the specimen. This reduced the computational cost and allowed for systematic variation of mesh density. Two modelling approaches were compared: the reverse-engineered NURBS surface with continuous curvature, and a linear polygon mesh directly derived from the scan data. As shown in Fig.  8 , the polygon mesh leads to significantly increasing stress concentration factors with decreasing element size, indicating mesh dependency due to artificial discontinuities. Fig. 8 a  Mesh sensitivity study for NURBS and polygon models.  b  Difference of the input geometries

In contrast, the NURBS-based model yields stable results beyond a certain level of refinement, highlighting the importance of smooth, continuous geometry for reliable stress analysis of 3D-scanned surfaces. The polygon mesh cannot produce consistent stress values even at very fine element sizes, since the numerically discretised geometry increasingly approximates the physical geometry, which contains clear edges resulting from the linear interpolation of the discontinuous point cloud.

To determine the required mesh resolution for subsequent simulations, both global and local element size criteria were evaluated. The global mesh density was defined such that the location of the maximum stress remained unchanged upon further refinement, whereas the local element size was assessed specifically at the notch with the smallest radius of curvature. The results revealed that a global element size of 0.2 mm and a local refinement to 0.05 mm are necessary to ensure mesh-independent results (see Fig.  8 a). These thresholds were used in all subsequent simulations.

The accurate reproduction of the failure location using a NURBS-based geometry confirms the predictive capability of the model, especially in comparison to idealised geometries or simplified 2D simulations.

According to Jahns [ 27 ], the ultimate tensile strength of the material examined under as-built conditions is 851 MPa. In the following, the fatigue stress concentration factor is used both to estimate the local stress amplitudes in the notched region and to estimate the fatigue life of the specimens. The local notch radii were determined using the curvature analysis function in Rhino, based on the NURBS-reconstructed surface geometry. This approach allows for the precise evaluation of local curvature along the as-built surface.

sections.heading: Numerical simulation
paragraphs: Overall, the static stress concentration factor successfully identified the crack initiation site in 6 out of 8 specimens, demonstrating the suitability of the numerical approach for capturing fatigue-critical surface features (see Table  4  in the Appendix), which lists the identification of failure. In the specimens where the crack initiation site could not be clearly identified numerically, the application of the fatigue stress concentration factor resulted in several notches exhibiting comparable stress levels. The applied load corresponds to the average cross-sectional area in the parallel section of the specimen, which ensures a uniform nominal stress distribution. As a result, the von Mises equivalent stress obtained from the finite element analysis directly represents the static stress concentration factor without the need for additional normalisation. The calculated fatigue stress concentration factors are subsequently used as input for the estimation model to estimate the fatigue life of the as-built specimens.

The analysis showed that the global mesh refinement was sufficient to initially identify the most critical notches on the as-built surface. These regions were partitioned and subsequently re-meshed with a locally refined element size of 0.05 mm to ensure that the stresses at the integration point do not change (see Fig.  8 ). This two-step approach allowed for efficient use of computational resources while maintaining the accuracy required for reliable evaluation of local stress concentrations.

sections.heading: Fatigue life estimation
paragraphs: To assess the impact of surface-induced stress concentrations on the fatigue life of as-built specimens, a numerical approach was used. Based on the previously calculated fatigue stress concentration factors and the material parameters derived from machined specimens, the model enables a local, geometry-based estimation of fatigue life. The estimation was performed based on the Basquin Eq. ( 7 ) [ 28 ]:

Figure  12 a shows the results of the fatigue life estimation, with the estimated fatigue life plotted against the experimentally determined life. It can be observed that most of the estimations fall within a scatter band of a factor of 3.0, indicating reasonable agreement between simulation and experiment. Most data points lie below the perfect fit curve, indicating that the model tends to underestimate fatigue life and therefore provides a conservative estimation. In Fig.  12 b, both the machined and as-built specimens are displayed in a combined S–N diagram. For the as-built condition, the local stresses, derived using the fatigue stress concentration factor, were used to represent the actual loading conditions. This allows for a direct visual comparison between both surface states, highlighting the impact of surface-induced stress amplification on fatigue performance. Furthermore, the 10% and 90% quantiles are indicated in the diagram, providing the variability of the experimental fatigue data.
Fig. 12 a  Fatigue life estimation.  b  S–N curve of local stress range for as-built and machined specimens with  m  = 4

The fatigue stress concentration factor provides a more physically meaningful approach for evaluating surface-induced stress concentrations in as-built specimens compared to static stress concentration factors. While static factors tend to overestimate the severity of local notches, often predicting unrealistically high stress peaks, the fatigue-based factor accounts for the effective influence of notch geometry under cyclic loading. Plasticity effects, such as local stress redistribution, particularly around small notches, can reduce the severity of these peaks, a behaviour that is better captured by the fatigue stress concentration factor.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The presented methodology demonstrates a combined numerical and experimental approach for assessing the influence of as-built surface topology on the fatigue performance of additively manufactured components. In the presented study, the NURBS-based surface reconstruction was implemented by dividing the as-built geometry into individual surface segments. An average NURBS surface edge length of 0.2 mm was selected, representing a compromise between capturing relevant surface features and computational effort. The minimum required NURBS patch size for representing fatigue-relevant surface features was not determined in this study. Establishing such a threshold would be valuable for future investigations to ensure a consistent balance between geometric resolution and computational efficiency. Furthermore, a higher resolution of the 3D surface scan may require a finer NURBS patch size to accurately capture the increased level of geometric detail. Consequently, the investigation of the necessary scan quality is also of critical importance for future studies aiming to achieve a reliable and efficient workflow. A comparable NURBS size was also applied in the literature, indicating that the chosen resolution in this study is consistent with other approaches for representing scan-based surface geometries in numerical fatigue analysis [ 17 ].

The experimental data points marked as  invalid failure location  represent threshold values and are shown for completeness only. These specimens were excluded from all further evaluations, including fatigue life estimation and numerical simulation, due to their failure occurring outside the parallel section. All specimens that failed outside the parallel section fractured in the transition region. Failure occurring outside the parallel section represents a general challenge in fatigue testing, as also reported in the literature [ 10 ]. The failure in some specimens may be attributed to the radius between the parallel section and the clamping area. A small transition radius can lead to elevated local stress concentrations, potentially resulting in premature failure outside the test region. Therefore, increasing the radius could be a beneficial design modification to reduce the local notch effect and ensure crack initiation occurs consistently within the uniform parallel section. Overall, it can be seen that the stress concentration of the surface exceeds the notch effect provided by the transition radius.

Alternative approaches can be employed to account for the reduction in fatigue strength caused by local stress concentrations, particularly by considering microstructural support effects [ 19 ]. Examples include the theory of critical distance (TCD) or the support factor concept as defined in the FKM Guideline [ 29 ,  30 ]. These methods do not only consider the maximum stress at one point, but also take into account how the stress is distributed in the area around the notch.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Overall, the study demonstrates that accurate surface characterisation and geometry-based fatigue assessment are essential for evaluating the performance of as-built DED-Arc components. The proposed methodology enables a local and physically motivated estimation of fatigue behaviour, providing a foundation for future design and qualification strategies in additive manufacturing. In summary, the approach developed in this work highlights the potential of topology-based fatigue assessment using reverse-engineered surfaces.
